title: Denderu
author: Mohammed Babagana
desc: Mutton pierced all over with a knife, pepper paste pressed into the holes, and baked in a sand-and-mud oven called a Blaa for a minimum of twenty-four hours.
longDesc: Denderu is the one properly documented Kanuri dish and it is remarkable. Mutton is butchered into large pieces — head and abdominal parts excluded — seasoned and garnished, then pierced all the way through with a pointed knife so that pepper paste can be worked into the holes. It goes into a special sand and mud oven known in Kanuri as a Blaa, on an earthen pot above hot charcoal, and cooks for a minimum of twenty-four hours, which can extend to weeks depending on preference. It is ready when the meat is soft and has gone a bit dry and baked.
ingredients: Mutton, preferably — butchered into large pieces, head and abdominal parts excluded
Fresh pepper, made into a paste
// The source states no specific quantity is specified for any of these
equipment: Blaa — a sand and mud oven
steps: Butcher the mutton into large pieces, excluding the head and the abdominal parts.
Season and garnish the meat before oven preparation.
Pierce the meat throughout with a pointed knife.
Apply the pepper paste into the pierced meat, working it into the holes.
Place the meat in the special sand and mud oven — the Blaa — on an earthen pot above hot charcoal.
Cook for a minimum of 24 hours. It may extend to weeks depending on preference.
Denderu is ready to be served when the meat becomes soft, and gets a bit dry and baked.
chefTips: Piercing before the paste goes on is the whole technique. The holes are how a day's worth of seasoning reaches the middle of a large piece of meat.
Soft, and a bit dry and baked. That is the stated doneness cue and it is doing a lot of work across a cooking window that can run from a day to weeks.
Twenty-four hours is the minimum, not the target. The source is explicit that it extends to weeks depending on preference.
A Blaa is a sand and mud oven, and it is what makes this possible — low, even, enclosed heat from charcoal over a very long period.
The source states outright that no specific quantity is specified for any ingredient, which is unusual and honest. Build the seasoning and pepper paste to taste.
Without a Blaa, the nearest domestic approximation is a very low oven, around 90 to 110°C, in a covered clay pot — but that is an adaptation and not the documented method.
Head and abdominal parts are specifically excluded in the butchering.
commonMistakes: Skipping the piercing, so the seasoning never reaches the middle.
Cooking it at a normal roasting temperature.
Treating twenty-four hours as the maximum.
Including the head or abdominal parts.
Judging it done when it is merely tender rather than dry and baked.
sources: Adapted from 'Denderu: Kanuri's popular delicacy', byline 'ByMohammed Babagana Manga & Edmond Lemdi Okolie, Maiduguri', Daily Trust. Kanuri local name: Denderu.

THE SOURCE ITSELF DECLARES THE ABSENCE OF QUANTITIES, which is unusual and worth quoting verbatim: 'Meat (preferably mutton), Salt, Maggi cubes, Royco cubes, fresh pepper, Onions (large one's), Curry powder and Garlic (optional) and will be used as desired and no specific quantity is specified.'

Method as printed: butcher the mutton into large pieces, excluding the head and abdominal parts; season and garnish before oven preparation; pierce the meat throughout with a pointed knife; apply pepper paste into the pierced meat; place the meat in a special sand/mud oven known as 'Blaa' on an earthen pot above hot charcoal; cook for a minimum of 24 hours, which may extend to weeks depending on preference.
DONENESS CUE, verbatim: 'Denderu is ready to be served when the meat becomes soft, and gets a bit dry and baked.'

Named people in the article: Ya Chellu, Ya Aji, Adebayo Ganiu, Ngozi Chukwuma, Hajja Mairam Babagana, Falmata Modu, Chris Skill. Place: Maiduguri, Borno State, and the Shehu's Palace. Occasions: Fridays at the palace, Eid el Kabir, marriages, naming ceremonies. Yield not specified.

THIS IS THE ONLY PROPERLY DOCUMENTED KANURI DISH FOUND, and the Kanuri record is otherwise close to empty. KALWA returned ZERO Nigerian results — every result was a South or Southeast Asian dried-fish dish, the phonetic collision with Sri Lankan karawala swamping the query entirely. KARASSU returned NOTHING. Kanuri dried fish preparations generally are undocumented, which is striking given that Borno's Lake Chad fishery underpins a major dried-fish trade. Those dishes were specifically sought and are not published.

A ROUTE TO MORE, recorded for the future: Voice of Nigeria, the federal broadcaster, published 'Borno Revives Indigenous Cuisine Through Youth Training', byline Nura Datti, Maiduguri. It names NO dishes in local language and gives no ingredients or processes, but it names two people worth pursuing — Dr Zanna Hassan Boguma, Senior Special Adviser to the Borno State Governor on Culture and Regional Integration, and Hajiya Hajjaghana Sulaiman, lead facilitator and President of the Kanuri Women Association. Borno will not yield to web search; an organisation whose president runs cuisine training is the obvious next step.
The domestic-oven adaptation suggested in the tips is labelled as an adaptation and is not from the source.
storage: The cooking method is itself a preservation. A week refrigerated once cooked.
reheating: Low oven, briefly. It is already dry by design.
healthBenefits: Very high in protein and very low in carbohydrate.
The long slow bake renders out most of the fat.
Mutton is rich in iron, zinc and B12.
culturalNote: Denderu is served on Fridays at the Shehu's Palace in Maiduguri, and at Eid el Kabir, marriages and naming ceremonies. A minimum twenty-four-hour bake extending to weeks is not documented anywhere else in Nigerian food writing, and the Blaa — a purpose-built sand and mud oven — is the kind of equipment that only exists where a technique has been refined over a very long time.
